shift/map: A filter slid over an image gives a map of how well each patch matched it. This map has one strong match, a nine, among weak ones.
shift/move: Shift the image one pixel to the right, and the map shifts with it. Nearly every number changes, though what the filter found has only moved one pixel.
shift/pool: Pooling fixes that. Cut the map into two by two windows, and keep only the largest value in each: nine, two, three and four. That is max pooling.
shift/same: Now shift the image again. The nine moves, but stays inside its window, and so does every window's largest value. The pooled output does not change at all.
shift/keeps: So max pooling keeps how strongly the filter matched in each window, and lets go of exactly where. That is the name: each window's values are pooled into one.
shift/cells: The idea comes from the brain. In 1962, Hubel and Wiesel described complex cells in the cat's visual cortex, which answer to an edge at one angle anywhere in a larger patch.
shift/later: Fukushima's neocognitron, in 1980, built that in, so a pattern still registered when it moved a little. In 1999, Maximilian Riesenhuber and Tomaso Poggio made the case for the max: the largest value still signals the best match.
max/grid: Now the numbers, on that same map: one channel, four by four. Its two by two windows do not overlap: each starts two cells after the last, a stride of two.
max/max: Max pooling keeps each window's largest value. Read row by row, that is nine, two, three and four.
max/out: Four by four becomes two by two: half as tall, half as wide, and a quarter of the numbers for the next layer to read.
max/map: Count rows and columns from zero. The three is output row one, column zero. Its window is input rows two and three, columns zero and one.
max/rule: Each output row covers two input rows: output row i covers input rows two times i and two times i, plus one. Columns work the same way.
max/avg: Average pooling takes each window's mean instead. The top left window adds up to eleven, and eleven over four is two point seven five.
shape/channels: A layer's output has one channel per filter, and pooling runs on each channel on its own. Sixteen channels of thirty two by thirty two become sixteen of sixteen by sixteen.
shape/formula: The height and width follow the output size formula, with a window size F of two and a stride S of two: thirty two minus two, over two, plus one, is sixteen.
shape/overlap: Windows may also overlap: three by three, with a stride of two, so each shares a column with the next. Twenty seven wide becomes twenty seven minus three, over two, plus one: thirteen.
shape/none: And pooling learns nothing. A filter's weights are its parameters: the numbers a layer learns, which set what it finds. A max or an average is a fixed rule, so pooling has zero parameters.
